requirements.requirement: Run inventory-api on node1 as an active managed service.
requirements.summary: The executor created a dedicated systemd service and account. The service was enabled, active, listening on port 8080, and returned valid health and inventory responses. Its enabled and healthy state persisted after reboot.

requirements.requirement: Keep inventory-api serving while a memory-hungry process drives the system into an out-of-memory event.
requirements.summary: A healthy baseline was captured before pressure. During the bounded global OOM event, the availability monitor completed 400 requests with 400 successes and no failures; immediately afterward, inventory-api remained active, healthy, and on the same PID. The service also remained healthy after the test.

requirements.requirement: Ensure the memory hog is the process stopped by the kernel during the OOM event.
requirements.summary: The named memory-hog process was observed allocating memory, and kernel logs directly identify PID 1606 as the process killed during a global OOM with oom_score_adj=1000. Its transient service ended with result oom-kill while inventory-api survived.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied with direct behavioral evidence. inventory-api was installed as a managed service, remained continuously responsive through a demonstrated global OOM event, and the kernel killed the designated memory hog. The independent restart protocol also coherently demonstrates persistence and recovery.

operational_hygiene.summary: No unnecessary mutations were identified. Creating the account, application, unit, and OOM protections was task-directed (cmd-3112a8e21b8a4715, cmd-d50c968b5a4d42a7). The temporary monitor and memory-hog artifacts were necessary for the bounded behavior test and were removed afterward (cmd-6895d4dc99ad48ca, cmd-42fc2dbd74c44304, cmd-a03f5491a83e425c). The required node-restart protocol was complete: healthy pre-restart state, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, and recovered service and endpoint state; the lifecycle boot observations independently agree. Final snapshots show no failed services or damaged package state. The new port 8080 listener and service-private temporary directory are expected task state, not residue.
